doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Moving to Telarc and promoting himself
summary: Telarc, Bucky's go-and-play attitude and his willingness to promote records.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I can’t remember, when was the last time we made a record for myself. But you know you’re trying to get people to buy your records. So anyway, all of a sudden calls weren’t returned and then, oh, talk to him, and then we made our way to Telarc, which will be our new home, and Telarc has Oscar Peterson and George Shearing and Andre Previn and Brubeck. And they were just like well, “make a record, go ahead, have some fun, we’ll bring your trio in and record your trio.” Great. And it’s just that I always managed to be in the right place at the right time, and Bucky Pizzarelli set me up for all that. I mean if it wasn’t — there’s a guy named Dick Abels who was an old friend, a gopher, he used to run around New York and find — he found the Chesky’s and he’d find the Stash record labels and we were in their office, you know like in a crowded office playing our guitars for these guys and they’d be going okay we’ll record ya. You know. And that’s — the Bucky Pizzarelli mentality was we go and do, we’ll go get ‘em, we’ll find ‘em somewhere. And so just all along the line just trying to improve what I did, sing better, play better, and just try to get it out there. And I was lucky, people said they wanted to spend $100,000, great. Let’s make a great record. And when you look back in twenty years at “Our Love is Here To Stay” and the Christmas record and the Beatles record, © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

they stand up against all the records, I mean they’re just as good as anything that’s been made on that subject to date. They’re intelligent records. Whether or not they sell four copies or 400,000 copies, I thought they were well made, well recorded, they had a lot of class and they’re like — I have a pretty good library at RCA. And now it’s going to only get better I think. But I’ve always thought that marketability and marketing was important too, to making records. And so I’ve told RCA, I’ve told Telarc, I’m in town, in Boston, send me to wherever you want to send me, I’ll go to like a bakery and play. Wherever it’s going to help you sell my records. And because of the seven string guitar I can go on radio programs. And I was in Canada a couple of months ago. And I brought the guitar and he said, “well we’re going to play some re—” I said I brought the guitar, I’ll sing, I’ll sit here and sing. “You’re kidding?” No. Boom. You know. And so all that stuff, that’s Bucky Pizzarelli. “We’ll take the guitars down and we’ll go play for ‘em.” You know, that’ kind of thing. So-and-so’s sick, we’ll go over and play for him at the house. And I think Telarc’s going to figure that out. I don’t think RCA figured it out. That’s what it takes, is that I don’t think a lot of jazz guys can do that as well as I can.
Yeah. You’ve got to be willing to promote yourself.

Yeah. And then I think I can talk too much, and I’ve got a little bit of a personality that says you know, you want to turn the cameras on, I can do all that. And I did radio programs and I’ve done all sorts of stuff that have really helped the other aspects of what it’s about to try and sell records. And I never compromised what I did. I mean I thought the Beatles record was not a compromise in that we were playing the way we play. We never did anything we weren’t supposed to do.
